113.title: Ash Wednesday: dust
113.hook: ashes on the forehead and the words: remember you are dust (Genesis 3:19)
113.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday, Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others go to church to receive a cross of ash on the forehead, with words recalling Genesis 3:19; Orthodox Christians begin Great Lent on Clean Monday instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany: strangers from the east, a river, a wedding. Your line was the light is for everyone. Now the circle turns darker.

One Wednesday in late winter or early spring, you might notice it on the train, at the office, in the grocery line: a dark smudge on someone's forehead. Sometimes a neat cross. Sometimes just a gray thumbprint. People who don't know lean over and say, hey, you've got something on your face. They know. It's there on purpose. That morning or at lunch, in a church, a minister or priest dipped a thumb in ash, pressed it to their forehead, and said a few words from the third chapter of Genesis, words about dust. A reminder worn in public, for one day. Today's word is the day it happens.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE TRAIN.` → `YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Ash Wednesday: the first day of Lent. Often the ashes come from burning the palm branches of last year's Palm Sunday, so last year's celebration becomes this year's dust. The words often echo what God says to Adam in Genesis. In the King James: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." That's blunt. Every life ends. In the Bible, ashes go with grief and turning around: Job, at the end of his long argument with God, says he repents "in dust and ashes." But go back one chapter in Genesis, to how the first human was made: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Readers of the Hebrew hear a pun. The human is adam. The ground is adamah. An earthling, from the earth. So being dust isn't only bad news. It's what God picked up, and shaped, and breathed into. A psalm puts it tenderly: "he remembereth that we are dust." Not as a threat. As someone who knows how fragile you are. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists keep Ash Wednesday, and some other churches do too. Orthodox Christians don't; their Great Lent begins on a Monday called Clean Monday, after an evening when people ask one another's forgiveness. For Christians, the ash points two ways: you are dust, and you are loved.

segments.voice: Press a finger into a plant's soil, touch the earth outside, or just look closely at the back of your hand, and remember you're made of the same stuff as the ground. You won't be here forever; let that be true without panicking, and feel your breath going in and out. If you pray, remember the other half, breathed into and loved; if you don't, simply hold both at once: fragile, and here.

114.title: Lent: forty days
114.hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving, echoing Jesus in the desert
114.howItsDone: During Lent many Christians fast in some way, pray more and give to the poor; Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on Fridays, Orthodox Christians traditionally fast from meat, dairy and eggs through Great Lent, and some Protestants give up or take up one personal practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday, and your line: dust, and loved. The ash opens a season. Today, what comes next.

Every spring you hear it at work, at school, in group chats: so what are you giving up for Lent? Chocolate. Coffee. Social media. Swearing. One person gives up nothing and says they're giving up giving things up. It can sound like a second round of New Year's resolutions. But the season started somewhere much older and harder. In the Gospels, right after his baptism, Jesus goes out into the wilderness alone, and stays. The King James says, "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." Hungry, alone, tested, in the desert. Today's word is the season Christians built around those forty days.
screen: `WHAT ARE YOU GIVING UP?` → `INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Lent. The English name is usually traced to an old word for spring, the season when the days lengthen. In Greek and Latin it's simply called the fortieth. Forty is a number the Bible keeps returning to: forty days of rain for Noah, forty days for Moses on the mountain, forty years for Israel in the wilderness, forty days for Elijah walking to the mountain of God, and forty days for Jesus in the desert. Readers hear forty as the Bible's number for a long, testing stretch that changes people. Lent is traditionally made of three practices, from Jesus's own teaching in the Sermon on the Mount: prayer, fasting and giving to the poor. He doesn't say if you fast. He says when. Churches keep it differently. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and abstain from meat on the Fridays of Lent. Orthodox Christians traditionally keep a fast without meat, dairy or eggs through Great Lent. Some Protestants choose something personal, or take something up instead: reading a Gospel, volunteering, calling someone each day. Some churches don't mark Lent at all. Underneath sits a shared idea: giving something up isn't a punishment. It's meant to make room. The hour you'd spend scrolling becomes an hour for prayer. The money you'd spend on coffee goes to someone who needs it. Some say the hunger itself reminds them what they're really hungry for. Christians call it a season of preparation, clearing space for Easter.
screen: `LENCTEN: SPRING.` · `FORTY: THE BIBLE'S TESTING NUMBER.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LESS, TO MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: It doesn't have to be Lent right now: ask what's taking up too much room in your days, a habit, a screen, a snack, a complaint you keep repeating, and choose one small thing to set down for a week, or one to take up in its place. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can offer it to God; if you don't, just notice what fills the space.

115.title: Palm Sunday and Holy Week
115.hook: branches in, a cross by Friday; the week the whole year turns on
115.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday many churches bless and hand out palm branches, walk in procession and read the Passion; through Holy Week Christians gather for services each day toward Easter, and many walk the Stations of the Cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lent, and your line: less, so there's room. Lent walks toward one week. Today, it arrives.

Jerusalem, a few days before Passover. The city is packed with pilgrims, and Roman soldiers are watching the crowds. A man comes over the Mount of Olives riding a young donkey. Not a warhorse. A donkey. And the crowd goes wild. People throw their cloaks on the road in front of him. Others cut branches from the trees. John's Gospel says they "Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord." It feels like a parade, like the beginning of something. And by Friday of that same week, he'll be on a Roman cross. Today, the week everything turns on.
screen: `PASSOVER, A PACKED CITY.` → `A DONKEY, NOT A WARHORSE.` → `BRANCHES AND CLOAKS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the shout. Hosanna sounds like praise, and became praise, but began as a plea, from Hebrew in Psalm 118: save, please. Save us now. The crowd is shouting praise and a prayer for rescue at once. And the donkey matters. The prophet Zechariah had pictured Jerusalem's king coming humble, riding on a donkey. Jesus seems to choose that picture on purpose: a king, but not the kind with an army. In the Gospels, Jesus clears the traders out of the temple. He teaches in its courts. A woman anoints him with costly perfume. On Thursday, a last supper with his friends. On Friday, the cross. On Saturday, silence. On Sunday, the empty tomb. People have long noticed how fast it turns, from palms to a cross in five days. Sometimes they say the same crowd that shouted hosanna shouted crucify, but the Gospels don't say who was in either crowd. Christians keep this week as the center of the whole year. On Palm Sunday, many churches hand out palm branches and walk in procession, then read the long story of Jesus's death, the Passion, so the whole week is felt at once. In Russia and other places where palms don't grow, Orthodox Christians carry pussy willow branches instead. In many places, people walk the Stations of the Cross, praying at fourteen scenes along the way to the cross. And in Jerusalem, pilgrims still walk down the Mount of Olives on Palm Sunday, waving branches, along roughly the road the donkey took.

116.title: Maundy Thursday
116.hook: from mandatum, commandment: love one another, and many churches wash feet
116.howItsDone: On Maundy Thursday churches in several traditions hold an evening service remembering the Last Supper, often with the washing of feet, and some end it by stripping the altar bare; some traditions practice foot washing at other times of the year as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hosanna, and your line: the week everything turns. Now, Thursday of that week: the last night.

An upstairs room in Jerusalem, evening. Supper is under way, Jesus and his disciples reclining at the table. Then the teacher stands up. He lays aside his outer robe, ties a towel around his waist, pours water into a basin, and starts washing his friends' feet, one by one. In that world, it was work for a servant, not a host. When he gets to Peter, Peter can't stand it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." So Peter, being Peter, swings the other way and asks him to wash his hands and his head too. Today's word is the name of that night.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM.` → `A TOWEL AND A BASIN.` → `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.`

segments.voice: Maundy. The name is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, commandment. Later that night, in John's Gospel, Jesus says: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another." In Latin, that sentence begins with mandatum, and it became the chant sung while feet were washed. And the commandment has a picture attached: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Love here isn't a feeling. It's a towel. It's kneeling, doing the job nobody wants. John tells the foot washing. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell what else happened that night: the Last Supper, when Jesus takes bread and wine and, in Luke and in Paul's letter, tells his friends to do this in remembrance of him. Christians understand that meal in different ways. Catholics and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in them; other Protestants of a spiritual presence, or a memorial. Churches that share communion trace it back to this night. Some churches still wash feet on Maundy Thursday. Popes have knelt to wash the feet of prisoners and refugees; in some churches, everyone takes a turn. In Britain, the monarch hands out special coins, Maundy money, to older people each year, a faint echo of the old custom. Then, in some churches, the altar is stripped bare. The night ends in a garden, with an arrest.

117.title: Good Friday
117.hook: churches strip altars, keep silence, and venerate the cross
117.howItsDone: On Good Friday churches are left bare and some Christians fast and keep silence; Catholics venerate the cross at an afternoon service without Mass, Orthodox Christians carry the epitaphios, an icon of Christ's burial, in procession, and some Protestants keep services from noon to three.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maundy: a towel, a basin, and your line: love one another. That night ended in a garden, with an arrest. Today is the next day.

On Good Friday, a church can look robbed. The altar is bare wood or stone. No flowers, no candles burning, the cloths gone. Often the bells stay silent. People come in without talking, and sit. Some services start at noon and run until three in the afternoon. Matthew writes: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." By the old way of counting the day, that's noon to three. So some Christians keep those hours, in silence, or with long readings, or a single hymn. Today's word is the day's strange name.
screen: `A CHURCH THAT LOOKS ROBBED.` → `NO CANDLES, NO BELLS.` → `NOON TO THREE.`

segments.voice: Good Friday. First, what the Gospels say happened. After his arrest, Jesus is questioned by the high priest's council, then handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate sentences him, and Roman soldiers crucify him outside the city wall. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for rebels and slaves, meant to be slow and public. His friends mostly scatter. Women who had followed him from Galilee stay, watching. In John's Gospel, his last words are three in English: "It is finished." In Greek, a single word: tetelestai. Not it's over, I give up, but complete, done, accomplished. Christians hear it as the end of a work, not a defeat. So why call the day good? Honestly, nobody is sure. Good may be the old English sense of holy; some suggest it came from God's Friday. The sources don't settle it. But Christians call it good because they believe something was done that day for the whole world, out of love, and they explain how in more than one way. Churches keep the day differently. Catholics celebrate no Mass; in the afternoon they read the Passion, and people come forward one by one to kneel before the cross, touch it, or kiss it. Orthodox Christians carry a cloth icon of Christ's burial in procession and lay it in a tomb decked with flowers. Some Protestants gather for three hours at noon, or for a service where candles are put out one by one, until the church is dark.
screen: `PILATE, SOLDIERS, A ROMAN CROSS.` · `TETELESTAI: IT IS COMPLETE.` · `WHY GOOD? NOBODY IS SURE.` · `THE CROSS, THE TOMB, THE DARK.`

segments.voice: For the next two minutes, keep silence: no music, no plans, no words. If you have a cross, you can look at it. If you pray, simply stay near it, the way the women stayed; if you don't, let the silence be for anyone who is suffering today.
Good Friday. The day Christians remember Jesus's death on the cross, with bare altars, silence and the veneration of the cross. Today's word.

118.title: Holy Saturday
118.hook: the quiet day; in the old vigil a new fire is lit in the dark
118.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday churches stay bare and quiet during the day; after dark churches in several traditions hold the Easter Vigil, lighting a new fire and the Easter candle and passing its flame from person to person, and Orthodox churches pass the light at midnight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Friday: a Roman cross, and your line: it is finished. Today is the day in between.

The day after a funeral has its own kind of quiet. The flowers are still there, the casseroles in the fridge. Everyone has gone home. The Gospels give this day almost nothing. Jesus has been laid in a new tomb cut in the rock, a great stone rolled to the door. Luke says the women went home, prepared spices to anoint the body, "and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment." Matthew adds only that a guard is posted and the stone sealed. Nobody in the story knows what comes next. Today's word is the name of that silence.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `A STONE ACROSS THE DOOR.` → `THEY RESTED THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Holy Saturday. For most of the day, churches stay bare and quiet, no celebration yet: a day for waiting in grief. But Christians have also wondered where Jesus was that day. The Apostles' Creed says, in the Book of Common Prayer, "He descended into hell." The First Letter of Peter says he "went and preached unto the spirits in prison." Out of those lines grew an old picture, sometimes called the harrowing of hell. In the Orthodox Easter icon, Christ stands on the broken gates of death, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their tombs by the wrists. Christians read that line of the creed in more than one way: some as a descent to the dead, some as a way of saying he truly died. Then night falls, and something happens in the dark. In the old Easter Vigil, kept by Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and others, people gather outside, or at the back of a dark church, and a new fire is lit. From it, one tall candle is lit, the Easter candle, and carried in slowly while someone sings: the light of Christ. People light small candles from it, then from each other, until the whole dark church is glowing. In Orthodox churches, it happens near midnight. Every light goes out. The priest comes out holding a single flame and invites everyone to come and receive the light, and it passes from candle to candle through the crowd, out into the street. John's Gospel has a line for it: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
screen: `A DAY OF SILENCE AND WAITING.` · `HE DESCENDED INTO HELL.` · `A NEW FIRE IN THE DARK.` · `CANDLE TO CANDLE, INTO THE STREET.`

segments.voice: Turn off the lights around you, or close your eyes, and let the dark be dark for a while, not knowing what comes next. Near the end, turn on one small light, light a candle if it's safe, or simply open your eyes, and watch how much one flame changes a room. If you pray, welcome it as a sign of what Christians wait for; if you don't, just notice the difference.
Holy Saturday. The quiet day between the cross and Easter, which ends in the dark with a new fire. Today's word.

119.title: Easter is fifty days
119.hook: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! Orthodox Pascha often falls on a later date, by the old calendar
119.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Easter, or Pascha, with services at dawn, at the vigil or at midnight, greeting one another with Christ is risen and the reply He is risen indeed; many churches keep the Easter season for fifty days, to Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday, and your line: light in the dark. This week walked a hard road: ashes, Lent, palms, a towel, a cross, a silent tomb. Seventeen weeks on the path. Today, the stone moves.

Midnight, outside an Orthodox church. Hundreds of people holding candles in the street, some of them kids way past bedtime. The priest steps out and calls, Christ is risen! In a Greek church, Christos anesti. The whole crowd shouts back: Truly he is risen! Again, and again, louder. Then fireworks, bells, and people kissing each other three times on the cheek. For weeks afterward, friends greet each other that way on the street, even in text messages. In English-speaking churches you'll hear: Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! It all goes back to a Sunday morning, and some women at an empty tomb, where an angel says, "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." Today's word is the feast's name in Greek and Latin.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, CANDLES IN THE STREET.` → `CHRIST IS RISEN!` → `HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Pascha, the Greek and Latin name for Easter, comes from the Hebrew Pesach, Passover. Jesus died and rose at Passover time, and the first Christians, who were Jewish, heard his death and rising as a new passing over, from death to life. Paul writes: "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." So in French, Easter is Pâques; in Spanish, Pascua. English says Easter, a word whose origin is still debated. The English reply echoes Luke: when two disciples rush back to Jerusalem, the others meet them with the news, "The Lord is risen indeed." Western churches keep Easter on the Sunday after the first full moon of spring, by their reckoning. Orthodox churches count by the older Julian calendar, so Orthodox Pascha often falls later, sometimes by weeks, and some years both land on the same day. Families with a foot in both traditions sometimes celebrate twice. And Easter isn't only a day. Like Christmas, it's a season, and a longer one: fifty days, all the way to Pentecost, with the candles burning and the alleluias going. For Christians, this is the center of everything. Paul put it bluntly: "And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain." That's the weight behind the shout.
screen: `PASCHA, FROM PESACH: PASSOVER.` · `THE LORD IS RISEN INDEED.` · `THE FULL MOON AND TWO CALENDARS.` · `FIFTY DAYS, NOT ONE.`
